title: The Short Long Way
summary: Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah, the sage no one could beat in an argument, discovers that a girl in a field and a boy at a crossroads are wiser than he is. A clever story about the wisdom of children and about listening all the way to the end.
pages: Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah was one of the greatest sages in Israel. He could answer any question, and even kings were amazed by him. But Rabbi Joshua liked to say: "No one ever beat me in an argument, except one woman, one girl, and one boy!" And here are two of those stories.

Once, Rabbi Joshua was walking along the road, and in front of him stretched a green field. Through the field ran a little path, and Rabbi Joshua walked along it to take a shortcut. A girl standing at the side called out to him: "Rabbi! This is a field! Why are you walking through it?"

"But there's a path here," answered Rabbi Joshua. "It's a trodden path. Lots of people have already walked on it."
The girl smiled and said: "That's true. And people like you, who took a shortcut through the field, are the ones who made it!"
Rabbi Joshua laughed. She was right: the path was made by people walking on someone else's field.

Another time, Rabbi Joshua was walking to a town he didn't know. He came to a crossroads, a place where the road splits in two. By the crossing sat a little boy playing with stones. "Boy," asked Rabbi Joshua, "which way goes to the town?"

The boy pointed and said: "This one is short and long, and that one is long and short."
Rabbi Joshua raised an eyebrow. What did that mean? He didn't ask any more. "If this one is short," he thought, "I'll take the short one!" And off he went down the first road.

And sure enough, after a short while he could already see the town. But then... oh no! The town was surrounded by gardens and orchards, with fences and thick trees, and there was no way through. He turned right and left, but he couldn't find an opening. In the end he had no choice: he walked all the way back to the boy.

"My son," said Rabbi Joshua, "you told me this road was short!"
The boy gave a mischievous smile: "And didn't I tell you it was also long?"
Now Rabbi Joshua understood: the first road was short to the town, but long until you could get inside. And the second one was longer, but it led straight to the gate.

Rabbi Joshua bent down and kissed the boy on the head. "Happy are you, Israel, for all of you are very wise, from the greatest to the smallest!" he said. In other words: how good it is for the people of Israel, everyone is wise, from the oldest grown-up to the littlest child.

And you? You also have clever questions and ideas that grown-ups never thought of. And maybe we learned one more thing from this story: it's worth listening all the way to the end before you run off. The road that looks the shortest is not always the fastest.
